name: Bremen
title: Bremen Ship Thickness Gauging | Weser Bulk and Breakbulk UTM
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging in Bremen's Weser docks for bulk carriers, breakbulk and project ships: holds, ballast tanks, decks, hatch covers, piping.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Bulk, Breakbulk and Project Cargo Ships in the Port of Bremen
intro: Bremen's own docks lie far up the tidal Weser, well inland of Bremerhaven, and they serve a different trade: steel, grain and feed, building materials, scrap and heavy project cargo carried by handy-sized bulk carriers, multipurpose ships and coasters. Those ships often spend days alongside while cargo is worked by crane or grab, which leaves time for hold, tank and deck gauging. Nobody from Atlantis is based in Bremen; for each ship, technicians fly in from India and work aboard under the master's permits.

highlights.h: Breakbulk and project ships, Neustädter Hafen
highlights.p: Multipurpose and heavy-lift ships loading steel, machinery and plant components lie alongside for days while each unit is lifted, lashed and stowed. Tween-deck plating, hatch covers, crane pedestals and tank tops under heavy units can be gauged as holds open and close.

highlights.h: Bulk discharge in the industrial harbours
highlights.p: Bulk carriers and coasters bringing raw materials, aggregates and scrap to the industrial harbours are emptied by grab. Once the last grab is out of a hold, its frames, brackets, hopper plating and tank top can be measured before the ship ballasts and sails.

highlights.h: Grain and feed ships at the silos
highlights.p: Agribulk cargoes for mills and feed producers are discharged at the grain and feed terminals in the city port. Holds on these ships must be clean and dry for every cargo, so the end of discharge is a natural point to check hold plating, frames and bilge wells.

port.h: Bremen's city docks on the upper tidal Weser
p: The city of Bremen lies on the Weser a long way upstream of the river mouth, and its port is reached after a pilotage passage up the Lower Weser past Bremerhaven, Nordenham and Brake. The river stays tidal as far as the weir at Hemelingen, above the city centre, so arrivals and departures of the deeper ships are timed to high water. Bremen's port areas lie mainly in the west of the city: on the right bank, the industrial harbours with their bulk and steel berths and the Holz- und Fabrikenhafen with grain, feed and warehouse quays; on the left bank, the Neustädter Hafen for breakbulk and project cargo. Downriver, Vegesack and Lemwerder on the opposite shore are known for yacht and naval building. bremenports manages the public port infrastructure of both Bremen and Bremerhaven.

Because the river limits draught, the ships that come up to Bremen are smaller than those at the container quays downstream: handysize and smaller bulk carriers, multipurpose and heavy-lift ships, general cargo ships, coasters and river-sea vessels. The cargo is the heavy, unglamorous kind that German industry runs on. Steel products arrive and leave over the Neustädter Hafen, where project cargo such as plant components, machinery and transformers is also loaded; raw materials, aggregates and scrap move through the industrial harbours; and grain and feed come in for the mills and compound feed makers of the region. The steelworks on the Weser in the north-west of the city generates ship traffic of its own. Ships that arrive too early for the tide or the berth usually wait downstream or off the Weser mouth rather than in the city.

What makes Bremen useful for gauging is time alongside. Breakbulk loading is slow, with every unit slung, lashed and surveyed, and a multipurpose ship can stay in the Neustädter Hafen for several days while a project shipment is assembled. Grab discharge of bulk opens the holds one after another. Owners and managers of multipurpose and handysize tonnage are well represented in north-west Germany, and their superintendents use those days for intermediate-survey preparation, owner's condition checks and hatch cover work without taking the ship off hire. In a hard winter floating ice can come down the Lower Weser, and autumn storms can hold ships at the river mouth, but once a ship is moored in one of the basins neither normally stops work on board.

facilities.h: Where a ship can be gauged in Bremen
p: Bremen is a cargo port rather than a repair port, and almost all gauging here is done afloat while the ship lies at a working berth. At the breakbulk quays of the Neustädter Hafen, the window opens when a hold has been emptied or before stowage starts, and access to tween decks and hatch covers follows the cargo plan. At the bulk berths in the industrial harbours, an empty hold is available as soon as the grab finishes, and the crew can usually ventilate a ballast tank or two while discharge continues elsewhere. Lay-by berths in the basins take ships waiting for cargo or orders, and those are the best places for longer jobs.

For dry-docking, ships trading to Bremen normally go downriver to the floating docks in Bremerhaven or to a yard elsewhere on the North Sea, and readings taken in the city can be handed to that yard as a steel estimate. Where a ship has a voyage repair arranged at a Bremen quay, gauging can run alongside it, for example to confirm how far the wastage extends around a damaged area, or which lengths of piping should be cropped out rather than patched.
list: Neustädter Hafen breakbulk and heavy-lift quays — hatch cover, tween-deck and tank-top gauging on multipurpose ships between loading stages.
Bulk berths in the industrial harbours — hold frames, brackets and hopper plating measured on bulk carriers once grab discharge is finished.
Grain and feed terminals in the city port — hold plating and bilge-well checks on agribulk ships at the end of discharge.
Lay-by berths in the port basins — longer owner's condition and pre-purchase surveys on ships waiting for cargo or orders.
Quays used for afloat voyage repairs — gauging around damaged structure and piping to fix the extent of renewal.
Floating docks downriver at Bremerhaven — the usual docking choice, with readings from the city used as the steel estimate.

context.h: Inspection rules and trades on the upper Weser
p: Port state control in Bremen, as in every German port, is carried out under the Paris MoU by the Ship Safety Division of BG Verkehr, the body that also handles flag state work for German-registered ships. The older handysize bulk carriers and general cargo ships that trade to river ports like Bremen are exactly the tonnage that the Paris MoU's risk-based targeting picks out, since age, ship type and inspection history all raise a ship's priority. Corroded hatch covers, air pipe heads and deck fittings appear again and again in deficiency lists for that kind of ship, and a pre-arrival check of those areas takes the crew a day and can spare the owner a detention.

Multipurpose and heavy-lift ships, which Bremen sees more of than most ports, have their own weak points. Tween-deck pontoons and hatch covers are lifted and re-stowed constantly, heavy-lift cranes load their pedestals and the deck around them, and tank tops take point loads under heavy units. Owners now reporting emissions under EU ETS (from 2024) and working to FuelEU Maritime targets (from 2025) are asking whether these older ships justify another survey cycle, and thickness data on decks, covers and holds feeds that decision. Under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, every ship calling here, whatever its flag, must also carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs on Bremen's bulk and breakbulk ships
jobs.p: Jobs in Bremen follow the slow rhythm of breakbulk and bulk handling. Instead of racing a terminal window, the team usually works hold by hold behind the cargo operation, with the chief officer releasing spaces as they are emptied or before they are loaded. Multipurpose ships bring hatch cover, tween-deck and crane work; bulk carriers bring hold and wing-tank structure; ships waiting for orders bring longer condition surveys. Scopes are agreed with the superintendent before the ship comes up the river, and readings are shared daily, so decisions about the next docking can be taken while the ship is still alongside. Typical examples:
list: A multipurpose ship loading project cargo at the Neustädter Hafen: hatch cover top plates and girders, coamings and tween-deck pontoons gauged ahead of an intermediate survey.
A handysize bulk carrier after grab discharge in the industrial harbours: side-shell frames, lower brackets, hopper and topside tank plating, with tank-top pitting recorded.
A heavy-lift ship before a large lift: deck and pedestal structure around the cranes, with magnetic particle testing at the pedestal welds.
A general cargo ship idle at a lay-by berth: owner's condition gauging of ballast tanks, double bottom and air pipes for a prospective buyer.
A river-sea coaster discharging grain: deck, hatch coaming and hold plating readings to plan steel before her next docking.

logistics: Bremen Airport is within the city, not far from the port areas, and has European connections; Hamburg Airport offers more long-haul choice and is linked to Bremen by rail and motorway. The ship's agent arranges ISPS access to the terminal and confirms the berth, which matters in Bremen because a ship can shift between basins during a call. The technicians from India travel on Schengen visas, so please send expected arrival dates early; mobilisation is then fixed against the ship's river passage and berthing time.

faqs.q: Can hatch covers be gauged while a multipurpose ship is loading in Bremen?
faqs.a: Yes, if the cargo plan leaves them open or stacked for long enough. Top plates, side plates and girders are measured with the covers open or landed on deck, and coamings and compression bars are checked at the same time. On ships with folding or pontoon covers, the chief officer usually sequences the holds so that one or two sets of covers are free at any moment, and the team follows that sequence.

faqs.q: Is there a dry dock in Bremen for a renewal survey?
faqs.a: Bremen is not where merchant ships go for dry-docking. Ships leaving the city usually dock downriver at Bremerhaven or at another North Sea yard chosen by the owner. What Bremen offers is time alongside, so many superintendents use a call here to measure holds, ballast tanks and decks in advance, giving the docking yard a steel estimate before the ship arrives.

faqs.q: How does the tide on the Weser affect a gauging job?
faqs.a: The tide governs when deeper ships can come up the river and go back down, so a ship's arrival and departure can move by hours. Once she is moored, the tide matters little to the work on board. We plan mobilisation on the agent's latest arrival estimate and order the scope by priority, so that a departure brought forward does not leave the most important spaces unmeasured.

faqs.q: Can cargo holds be gauged during grab discharge?
faqs.a: Not in a hold that is still being worked, because grabs, payloaders and falling cargo make it unsafe. A hold is gauged once discharge in it is complete and the stevedores have left, while cargo continues in the others. On a bulk carrier with several holds, that rolling sequence often allows the full hold scope to be finished within the normal length of the call.

faqs.q: Do you also gauge the river-sea ships and coasters that call at Bremen?
faqs.a: Yes. Smaller ships face the same survey requirements as larger ones, on a smaller scale: deck, hatch coaming, hold, ballast tank and double-bottom readings, plus piping where corrosion is suspected. Their crews are small, so opening and ventilating tanks takes careful planning with the master, and we keep the scope tight enough to finish during the call.
